title: [Cloudflare] Introducing Zero Wire, a hub for investigating critical Internet vulnerabilities
summary: You run security at your organization. It’s 7:00 am, and you’re having breakfast. You receive a ping: a new critical vulnerability has been disclosed. Your team scrambles to compare vendor advisories, read technical research, check which systems run the affected software, and answer familiar questions from the business: are we affected, and what are we doing about it? Another disclosure arrives before that work is finished.AI is changing both the volume and speed of critical vulnerability discovery. It can analyze large codebases at scale and surface deeply nested flaws that may have existed for years without being found through human review. That discovery momentum will put more pressure on security teams to understand the impact of each disclosure on their infrastructure.To help security teams prepare, today we’re introducing Zero Wire: a public vulnerability intelligence feed on Cloudflare Radar, bringing the clarity of a news wire service to critical security developments. It helps security leaders and practitioners understand significant vulnerabilities and decide what to do next.How it worksZero Wire lives inside Cloudflare Radar under the security section.Each briefing brings together a plain-language explanation of the vulnerability, who should investigate it, recommended actions, and links to the evidence and vendor guidance. The format is deliberately simple: an index card with what you need to know, without the drama. A CISO should be able to understand the issue quickly and ask the right questions. An engineer should be able to follow the same briefing to the technical guidance needed to investigate and remediate it.We also offer a pre-compiled prompt you can use with your agent to assess the impact on your infrastructure. Cloudflare contributes security research, observations from our network, and practical knowledge of the controls that can help reduce exposure. The information is useful whether or not you are a Cloudflare customer. Zero Wire brings that context together with authoritative external sources, giving readers a starting point for assessment and a place to return as an issue develops.Our focusRather than a catalog of every CVE, Zero Wire complements vendor advisories and vulnerability databases, linking readers to the evidence and technical guidance needed to act. Zero Wire focuses on critical CVEs in Internet-facing software, such as vulnerabilities in web applications, the runtimes and libraries they depend on, and services exposed to the Internet, where a proxy can help mitigate exploitation.We select significant issues that security teams need to understand and assess. Each briefing explains the potential impact, which deployments should be investigated, what is known about exploitation, and the available mitigation and patching guidance. A vulnerability’s severity and evidence of active exploitation are distinct: readers need both to make informed decisions.A dedicated Cloudflare protection, such as Web Application Firewall (WAF) rules, is not a prerequisite for inclusion. Some issues require vendor updates or changes beyond the traffic Cloudflare can inspect. Where Cloudflare controls can help, we explain their scope and configuration requirements.A walk through Zero WireStart on the Zero Wire homepage. Each card introduces an issue, identifies associated CVEs where applicable, and summarizes why it matters and what to do. You can search for a published briefing using a CVE or issue name, and follow technology tags to related entries. One briefing can cover several related CVEs when understanding them together makes the response clearer.Find what needs attentionThe homepage separates briefings into two categories. “Needs attention” brings together issues requiring active assessment or action, including those with known exploitation or developing guidance. “Reference” keeps briefings available when guidance has stabilized. Moving to “Reference” does not mean every affected system has been patched: an older vulnerability can still matter to an organization that has not completed remediation.The status and last-checked date help you interpret each card. Known exploitation, an ongoing investigation, and an available vendor fix describe different things. Read them alongside the briefing’s evidence rather than treating them as a verdict on your own environment.Understand what happened and who should investigateWhen you open a briefing, the overview tells you what happened, why it deserves attention, and which teams should investigate. The explanation connects the technical issue to its practical consequences, such as service disruption or risk of data exposure.For example, the recent php2shell vulnerability concerns flaws in the PHP runtime. That distinction matters for teams running applications such as WordPress or Magento: updating application code or a plugin alone does not repair the underlying runtime. The briefing helps readers identify the right system owners and directs them to the PHP security guidance for affected versions and remediation.Turn the briefing into an action planWhat to do now gives your team a short set of next steps. Depending on the issue, that can mean identifying affected deployments, checking versions with a hosting provider, applying vendor updates, reviewing suspicious activity, or keeping compensating controls in place while patching.The purpose is to make the next conversation concrete. For a PHP deployment, ask which runtime is actually running, whether the vendor’s fix has been applied, and who owns the update. Follow the linked vendor advisory for detailed applicability and remediation instructions, which can change as the investigation develops.Assess your exposure with an AI agentIn this section, we share a prompt that can be used with your AI agent to quickly assess the impact on your infrastructure. The prompt asks for a read-only assessment of deployed software, relevant vendor fixes, exposure, and compensating controls, with per-asset evidence, unknowns, and next actions. It helps your team investigate its own environment; copying the prompt does not itself scan or change systems.Check the evidence and follow what changedTo help you learn more about the vulnerability, each briefing links to external documents such as CVE records, research, and relevant exploitation evidence, including CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog. These sources answer different questions. A vendor advisory establishes affected versions and remediation guidance. An exploitation report provides evidence of attacker activity. If applicable to a briefing, Cloudflare can add context about traffic seen on our network, for example by showing traffic matching WAF rules that indicates exploitation attempts. Those distinctions matter. Observing an attack attempt does not establish that a particular organization was compromised. Equally, a lack of observed attempts on Cloudflare’s network does not establish that exploitation is absent elsewhere. Briefings distinguish what the sources establish from what remains unknown.Where available, charts add context to that evidence. The php2shell briefing shows the volume of HTTP requests matching Cloudflare WAF managed rules over time. Note that requests matching these rules are not a count of compromised systems or successful exploits; the chart aims at providing practitioners a sense of what the focus level is by threat actors on a particular vulnerability.Finally, update chronology records important developments, such as new advisories or changes to the evidence and response guidance. Together with the last-checked date, it helps returning readers understand what has changed since their previous visit.Understand Cloudflare’s roleThe Cloudflare section provides links to whether we offer compensating controls or provide a way to mitigate the vulnerability impact on your infrastructure. If a particular CVE can be addressed with a WAF rule, the briefing reports its availability and essential configuration requirements. When applicable, paid Plans and free Plans links take customers to the relevant dashboard configuration. The next step is explicit: “Review your WAF configuration to determine whether you are protected”. A link allows you to review your security posture, it does not automatically enable a rule or verify a deployment.Note that a WAF mitigation is a compensating control for the traffic it covers, it is not a replacement for fixing vulnerable software. Blocking the requests can prevent exposed data from reaching an attacker, but it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin. The security teams should always follow the vendor remediation guidance.Stay informed with Zero WireA useful vulnerability briefing should leave you with a clearer understanding of the issue and a concrete next step. Day Zero brings those essentials together: what happened, who should investigate, what to do now, and where to find the evidence.Visit Zero Wire vulnerability intelligence, share the relevant briefings with the teams responsible for your systems, and return for new entries and updates. When the next disclosure arrives, we want you to spend less time assembling the basic facts and more time acting on them.Follow Cloudflare Radar on X @CloudflareRadar and Bluesky @radar.cloudflare.com for updates.

title: [Cloudflare] How we halved DNS build delay and cut memory use by 85%
summary: When I last wrote about our DNS propagation pipeline in 2022, the Zone Builder received about 250 DNS record changes per second. Today it receives about 700, nearly three times as many, plus about 100 other events, such as zone setting changes. However, the number of events was never the real problem. The problem was the kind of work some of those events needed, and how that work grows with the size of a zone. Some zones now hold more than 20 million records, and we expect them to keep growing toward hundreds of millions.Each event starts a clock that measures how long it takes us to turn that change into data our authoritative DNS servers can use. We call that work a build. A build reads the current database state, converts it into the format used at the edge, and writes any changes to Quicksilver.In 2022, per-record builds were 150 times faster than full builds on average. On a test zone with one million records, per-record builds were 4,250 times faster. We ended that post with the obvious next step: do the same thing for zone settings.Why doesn't the Zone Builder just rebuild the setting that changed?It should, and that is where we ended up. However, proving when it was safe took most of the work. A record event identifies what changed. A zone event can come from many Cloudflare products, may not say why the zone changed, and can alter data shared by several zones with the same name. Choosing too much work wastes capacity. Choosing too little can leave stale or incorrect DNS data at the edge.We built a targeted build planner that chooses the smallest build we can prove is safe, and a new scheduler that combines work for the same zone. Zone setting changes no longer rebuild zones with tens of millions of records. Together, they cut peak memory by 85%, and the extra headroom let us safely shorten waits the pipeline has always needed for resilience, halving the time from a DNS change to its data being written to Quicksilver.How DNS changes reach the edgeA DNS zone is the collection of records and settings for a domain. Cloudflare uses a multi-stage pipeline to turn a change to that zone into data available across our global network.A customer changes a DNS record through the DNS Records API or dashboard, or another Cloudflare service changes a zone setting.The change is stored in a database.The database change or another system produces a Kafka event.The DNS Kafka Aggregator combines events from several Kafka topics and sends them to the Zone Builder.The Zone Builder reads the required zone data and converts it into keys understood by our authoritative DNS servers.The Zone Builder compares those keys with Quicksilver, our distributed key-value store. It writes only what changed, and Quicksilver propagates those changes across Cloudflare's network.This is a simplified view. The Zone Builder does not copy database rows directly to the edge. It combines records with zone settings, applies DNS serving rules, and organizes the result so our authoritative DNS servers can read it quickly.Why full builds stopped scalingThe original Zone Builder had one useful property: it did not need to know why a zone changed. It rebuilt the desired state from the current database state.Read the current zone and its settings.Read every DNS record in the zone.Convert those records into Quicksilver keys.Compare the new keys with those already stored.Remove stale keys, write changed keys, and update zone metadata.The final write contains only changed keys. However, a full build still reads, encodes, and compares every record, and holds the whole zone in memory while it does so. That is cheap for a small zone. For our largest zones, with tens of millions of records, the zone does not fit in memory at all. I explain how we handle that below.Zone settings made targeting harder. Universal SSL is one example. Enabling or disabling it updates metadata and can change Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) records at the zone apex, the bare domain, such as example.com. CAA records tell certificate authorities whether they may issue a certificate for the domain.A full build only needed to know that the zone changed. A targeted build must answer three questions:Which DNS names can change?Can shared metadata or the list of published zones change?What previous state must be removed from Quicksilver?Answering those questions safely meant solving five problems, which the rest of this post covers in order:Events had to say what changed.Each change had to map to the smallest build that is still correct.Builds had to account for data shared by every zone with the same name.The database could change between the event and the build.Combining work could not lose a Kafka message.Making events say what changedWe changed the event producer to include changed zone fields and settings, with previous and new values when available. We then traced each setting through the code that generates DNS output and classified what it could affect.Not every event was that specific. Some database functions only update a timestamp to say, in effect, "something about this zone changed." Sometimes that is harmless bookkeeping. Sometimes it means data changed elsewhere and must be read again.Those cases look identical in the event. Until we can identify the caller and its purpose, a timestamp-only update still causes a full build. The same rule applies to missing details, unknown events, or any change that may affect records anywhere in the zone. The planner never turns uncertainty into less work.Choosing the smallest safe buildQuicksilver output has two parts that matter here. Record keys contain the DNS answers for one zone and name. A smaller shared metadata key tells our authoritative DNS servers how to use that zone, including where to find special records such as nameservers and wildcards. Some events change only record keys; others must update both.With that distinction, the planner can choose one of five build types:Resources only: Rebuild the records at specific DNS names, which we call resources, without changing zone metadata. Ordinary A, AAAA, TXT, and CNAME changes usually take this path.Resources and metadata: Rebuild specific names and shared metadata. Nameserver and wildcard changes use this path.Apex and metadata: Rebuild the zone apex and metadata. Settings such as Universal SSL can use this path.Purge: Remove a zone that should no longer be published.Full zone: Rebuild every record when smaller work cannot be proven safe.The rule is simple: every key a targeted build writes must be byte-for-byte identical to what a full build would write. If we cannot prove that, we do a full build.Removing old state works as it did for per-record builds in 2022. Record events include deleted records and the previous version of updated ones. The Zone Builder then scans Quicksilver for the existing keys under each name it rebuilds, removing any that the new build did not write.Full builds remain necessary when a change can affect records anywhere in the zone or when a zone may need to be published for the first time.There is one deliberate exception. A full build holds every record from the database and every existing Quicksilver key for the zone in memory at once, and our largest zones do not fit. Above a fixed record-count threshold, the Zone Builder never escalates to a full build. It rebuilds the apex, the metadata, and every name identified by the queued events instead. We accept this tradeoff because a full build of those zones cannot finish, and, while it retries, it holds back every other change on its Kafka partition. Many of the cases that would otherwise need a full build involve several zones sharing one name, and zone holds reduce that risk by stopping the same name from being added to another account. For the rare cases that remain, such as enabling a zone on another network, we can manually rebuild individual names in the zone.When one name means more than one zoneQuicksilver stores each zone's record keys separately. It also stores one metadata key shared by every Cloudflare zone with that domain name. This shared key acts like a directory: it tells our authoritative DNS servers which internal zone IDs they may use when answering a query.Why can one name have several zone IDs? During customer onboarding, offboarding, and other lifecycle changes, multiple Cloudflare zone objects can briefly exist for the same public domain. We use a priority policy to choose a small, bounded set to publish.Consider four internal zones for example.com: Zone 101, Zone 202, Zone 303, and Zone 404. The metadata key currently lists Zones 101, 202, and 303. Zone 404 exists, but it is not selected. The numbers identify separate Cloudflare zone objects; customers still see one domain name.A TXT record change at www.example.com in Zone 202 affects only Zone 202's record keys, so the metadata key does not change. Nameserver and wildcard changes are different because the metadata key records information about them. Those builds must update both the zone's records and the metadata key.At execution time, the Zone Builder reads the current list again. If it writes the metadata key, it rebuilds the whole key from that fresh view rather than patching an older copy. It writes the triggering zone's records before the metadata that refers to them.Planning from the event, verifying before writingAn event describes what happened in the past. A build may wait while more events arrive and the database changes, so planning happens twice. The event first creates a conservative work list. Immediately before execution, the Zone Builder reads a fresh publication snapshot: the current zone settings, whether this Zone Builder should publish the zone to its network, and which same-name zone IDs belong in the metadata key. Here, a network is a separate, isolated copy of Quicksilver for one environment. Each Zone Builder deployment writes to one network, and a zone can be enabled on some networks but not others. For example, a zone can be served from Cloudflare's global network and also from the China Network.Fresh state can change the result in four ways:A targeted build can become a full build if the zone now has a feature that requires complete-zone work.A build can become a purge if the zone should no longer be published to this network.A build can be skipped if the triggering zone no longer belongs in the metadata key.A metadata build can reconstruct the shared key from the current candidate set.The fresh read comes from read-only copies of the database, called replicas, so builds do not compete with customer writes. Kafka delivery and database replication move independently: an event can arrive before its database change is visible on a replica. The DNS Kafka Aggregator delays events long enough to cover normal lag, and a final database check rejects the read if that replica is still behind.Combining changes in one schedulerRecord work and full-zone work previously used different schedulers. Each could combine its own work, but not work from the other scheduler. We replaced them with one unified scheduler. The planner decides what must be built, and the scheduler decides when it can run.When several events for one zone arrive before a build starts, the scheduler combines their work:An A record changes at www.example.com, requiring that name.A wildcard changes at *.example.com, requiring that name and shared metadata.The scheduler combines both names and the metadata update into one build.Merging only adds work. If any event requires the complete zone, the combined build becomes a full build. A purge overrides every rebuild because its desired result is that the zone is no longer published.The scheduler tracks two things separately: the DNS work that must be performed and the Kafka messages waiting to be acknowledged. A retry preserves both. Even when a full build or purge no longer needs the individual record names, the messages stay attached until the result is safely written.Keeping Kafka movingOne slow build can delay unrelated customers even when workers are available. Kafka divides messages into ordered partitions. For each partition, it stores one committed offset: the point before which every message is known to be complete. Moving that offset past unfinished work could lose a customer change after a restart.We use soft committing, which I previously described in my Secondary DNS deep dive. A build can finish out of order and be marked complete in memory, but Kafka's committed position advances only after every earlier message has also finished.In the diagram, message 2 is still running, so messages 3 through n cannot be committed. If the Zone Builder restarts, those in-memory completions disappear and Kafka replays messages 2 through n. We deliberately choose repeated work over losing a change.Targeted plans reduce how long the oldest message stays unfinished. The scheduler also prevents one busy zone from taking every worker. After a zone builds, its next build waits for a per-zone rebuild interval, which differs by Cloudflare plan. Changes that arrive in the meantime are merged into that next build. The scheduler normally enforces this interval, but lets old queued work run before it blocks a Kafka partition for too long. Zone locks and retry delays still apply, so a failing build cannot run in a tight loop.Releasing safelyA smaller build is useful only if it produces the same DNS data. We added equivalence tests for nameserver, wildcard, and apex paths. Each test runs a full build and a targeted build from the same database state, pins time-dependent values, and compares every Quicksilver key owned by the targeted plan byte for byte. Planner and scheduler tests cover classification, same-name zones, merging, purges, and escalation.During rollout, we also ran a full build next to every targeted build and compared the output. It was expensive by design, reading the complete zone every time, so we used it only until the mirror comparison below gave us the same confidence.Tests cannot reproduce every customer combination, so every release also runs through a mirror Zone Builder. It consumes the production Kafka stream and reads production database state, but writes to a separate Quicksilver environment that serves no customer traffic.A comparer checks a 20% sample of zones for missing keys, extra keys, and different values. The two environments do not always build a zone at the same instant, so a temporary mismatch is not automatically a regression. We look for new types of differences that remain after both pipelines catch up. That gives us confidence that targeted builds produce the same output as production.We built the DNS Mirror Dashboard to group those differences and keep examples for investigation. Naturally, it runs on the Cloudflare Developer Platform: a Worker receives results, Durable Objects maintain state, and Cloudflare Access protects it. The critical groups in the screenshot below were each checked and confirmed safe before release. The diff rate is the share of compared zones where production and mirror disagreed on at least one key at the moment of comparison. Most of those are timing differences that disappear once both pipelines catch up, so we watch two things: that the rate stays low, and that no new kind of difference appears.After the mirror results remained healthy, we rolled the scheduler out by a hash of the zone name. Hashing the name rather than the zone ID kept every zone sharing a name on the same scheduler, so two schedulers never wrote the same metadata key. We increased the percentage for free zones, then repeated the process for paid zones.ResultsOver 24 hours, we measured 86.81% of builds as resources only, 2.54% as resources and metadata, 2.30% as apex and metadata, and 1.30% as purges. Together, 92.95% of builds avoided rebuilding the complete zone. Full builds were the remaining 7.04%.The two metadata build types were full builds before, even for large zones. Together, they account for 4.84% of builds. Combined with the 7.04% that are still full builds, that is 11.88%, so full builds fell by about 40%. Their share of the count also understates the work avoided, because they include the largest zones. The full builds that remain average 0.35 seconds, because the events that still trigger them, such as a zone being published for the first time, mostly affect new zones with few records.In 2022, we also planned a batching system. The unified scheduler makes it unnecessary: it does not wait to form batches, and it merges events only when work is already queued for the same zone. Before, long full builds held back the committed offset for their partition. With fewer of them, we now consume Kafka at the rate events arrive, instead of falling behind and catching up in bursts of up to 1,550 messages per second.We also measured build completion delay: the time from a DNS record or zone setting change until the Zone Builder finished writing to Quicksilver. It does not include Quicksilver's distribution across our network, which varies by location and is unaffected by this work. Production ran the old schedulers, and the mirror ran the unified scheduler on the same events over the same 24 hours. The two environments are identical apart from the code: they consume the same Kafka events, read from the same database, and write equivalent data to Quicksilver. That makes this a controlled, side-by-side comparison. The figures combine every build type and customer plan, so they are not a latency guarantee for an individual zone. A large share of this time is the rebuild interval described earlier, not build work. At each measurement point, p99 is the time within which 99% of events finished. Typical delays barely changed here, because most builds were already small. The difference is in the tail: the largest p99 spike fell from 14.6 minutes to 1.21 minutes, a 12-fold reduction. The chart uses a logarithmic scale.Targeted builds also load complete large zones far less often. Aggregate working-set memory, the memory actively used by the deployment, fell from an average of 49 GiB to 7 GiB, an 86% reduction. Peaks fell from 79 GiB to 12 GiB, an 85% reduction.Those were the immediate results of the new scheduler. They also let us revisit two safeguards. The first is the rebuild interval, which stops one busy zone from rebuilding constantly and taking capacity from everyone else. With builds now cheaper, and far fewer of them reading complete zones, we could safely shorten that interval on most plans. The second is how long the DNS Kafka Aggregator holds each event, to make sure database replicas have caught up before we read from them. Once our databases began rejecting reads from replicas that had fallen behind, that buffer could safely be smaller. Together, these halved the median build completion delay, from about 7.7 seconds to about 3.3 seconds. In the chart below, the first step down is the DNS Kafka Aggregator change. The red band marks the Zone Builder release with shorter rebuild intervals. That release rolled out gradually across our servers, so the delay falls in two further steps rather than all at once.The p90 and p99 lines in that chart are less precise than they look. The histogram had buckets at 1, 5, 10, and 30 seconds, and a percentile that falls between two edges is estimated as if delays were spread evenly across that range. Most delays sit near the bottom of their range, so those estimates come out high: p99 reads close to 30 seconds, and p90 above 7 seconds. The exact average, which does not depend on buckets, confirms the halving. We have since switched to a native histogram, which chooses fine-grained buckets automatically. It puts p90 at about 5.5 seconds and p99 at about 12 seconds.Why full builds still existIn 2022, we said we planned to eliminate full builds entirely. We now know that is neither realistic nor useful. A zone being published for the first time needs every record written. A change that can affect records anywhere in the zone needs every record checked. An event that does not say what changed still gets a full build, because the planner never turns uncertainty into less work. For a small zone, a full build is also cheap.As we learn what more events change, we will keep moving them to targeted builds. However, the biggest gain has already landed: the events that used to rebuild our largest zones no longer do, and the full builds that remain are mostly triggered by events, such as first publication, that affect new, small zones.Want to know what happens after the Zone Builder writes a change? Read how Quicksilver distributes configuration to every Cloudflare data center in seconds.

title: [Cloudflare] 4 real? Tracking exploitation and patching of eMudhra’s weak keys
summary: On October 19, 2026, we learned about eMudhra’s eight shockingly weak keys: where eMudhra was trusted to pick a 115-digit number for their virtual combination lock protecting the Internet, they picked the number 4. Not even four digits, just the number 4. The other seven keys were similarly weak: 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237.The next day, we wrote a blog post on the immediate action we took to mitigate this leak, and what customers needed to do on their end to stay secure. Now, we are sharing a more in-depth follow up on the evidence we’ve seen of exploitation, and the progress seen on visitors patching their systems.Let's start with the scale of the problem. A certificate authority (CA) with weak keys this serious is unprecedented, and the potential consequences are significant. While there have been plenty of compromised certification authorities in the past (such as DigiNotar, TÜRKTRUST, and TrustWave), access to their keys has always been contained to a degree; these incidents gave a limited set of attackers or organizations the ability to issue fraudulent certificates. The eMudhra incident is fundamentally different; the affected intermediate private keys could be recovered almost instantly by anyone from the public certificates themselves. Anyone can independently recover these same signing keys and create certificates for any domain that an unpatched client not enforcing Certificate Transparency would accept.eMudhra announced they’re exiting the public CA business and have claimed a mistake in a key generation script, but have not yet shared the script. They signed a certificate revocation list (CRL) with what might’ve been a correctly generated key, and subsequently corrected it to be signed with the weak key.How did that come to be and why didn’t that set off alarms? Much has to be cleared up, including the role of the auditors and cross signers. This blog proposes the fixes and next steps for organizations to ensure they are secure.Patching CloudflareOur primary concern remains the security impact on Cloudflare, our customers, and the Internet as a whole. At the time of writing, all high priority Cloudflare systems have been patched. A small number of confirmed low impact tickets is being worked on.We started patching high-impact systems immediately on October 19. These included customer origin-facing proxies using Pingora, responsible for most of our outbound connections. These were patched in hours to reject the vulnerable eMudhra keys. At the same time, we started an AI-assisted analysis of our source code to find all other systems that trust these weak keys. Within four hours we had a full analysis. We assigned a ticket with preliminary analysis for each system, and asked the team to confirm and/or adjust the analysis before the end of the day. Where high impact was identified, we asked to patch immediately, and for the lower impact, remediation was due at the end of last week.Has Cloudflare seen exploitation across its network?To track whenever a customer’s server (or attacker) presents a certificate signed by eMudhra’s weak keys, we added logging to Pingora. As this outbound service accounts for the vast majority of outgoing TLS connections from a Cloudflare machine, any attacker attempting to snoop using the eMudhra keys would trigger this logging. The logging finished rolling out October 21.At the time of writing, a week later, we’ve seen about 22,000 attempted handshakes with the weak eMudhra keys. Two-thirds of the attempts were fetches of test sites such as emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com (which we mentioned in the developer guidance in our earlier post). Almost all of the remaining third went to origins who appeared to set up a certificate for themselves using the weak intermediate. Every handshake configured to verify the certificate was refused, as we already patched.About 160 of these handshakes stood out: the certificates’ Subject Alternative Names (SANs) were naming other organizations’ domains, unrelated to the Server Name Indication (SNI) requested in the handshake. Some of those names were domains related to consumer IoT devices. We noticed as well that those forged certificates were made after the keys leaked and some were valid for over two years, longer than any public CA may issue. However, these certificates looked like the servers' own default certificates rather than part of an attempt to intercept our connections. They named domains other than the ones being connected to, so they would have failed hostname verification anyway. And in several cases, a server presented the same certificate to connections from many of our locations, which means it came from the server itself rather than from something on a single network path.Thus while there is no evidence of the weak keys being used to intercept Cloudflare's connections so far, these keys appear to have been used to forge certificates within hours of the weakness becoming public: one of the forged certificates we saw was dated October 20 at 18:19 UTC, less than an hour after Mozilla's bug report was made public. This does not exclude carefully targeted interception. For that we have to rely on the usual indirect signals of system compromise — and so far, we have not seen any such signals.How many visitors are still vulnerable?So much about patching Cloudflare, but what about our visitors? We cannot directly test whether a visitor still trusts the weak keys without breaking connections, so we have to do something more indirect. For that we used our challenge pages:We rolled out an update to send out two probe connections on a fraction of challenge pages: one probe to ca1.cloudflarecaptcha.com and one to ca2.cloudflarecaptcha.com. Initially we installed an eMudhra signed certificate on ca1.cloudflarecaptcha.com and a regularly signed certificate on ca2.cloudflarecaptcha.com as control. Then we record whether these probes succeeded. This allows us to see if visitors that are served a challenge page still trust the weak eMudhra keys.What did we find? With 50 million probes over the last week, we see this:Big caveat upfront: by design the traffic to these challenge pages is highly skewed. There are many (unconfirmed) bots in there. Also, only clients that execute JavaScript (like browsers) will send probes.The jump in the data is due to the following changes—all times are UTC:October 23 15:30, we changed our control endpoint to also serve an eMudhra certificate, but this time without signed certificate timestamps (SCTs). There were some differences in acceptance, but not large. We could’ve added a new endpoint, but that would’ve required a slow release of our challenge platform. Changing the endpoint was easier.October 23 16:30, our challenge platform rolled back to a previous version because of an unrelated issue. The probes returned October 27 at 10:00.October 27 16:37, we noticed we did not send the G3 cross-sign, which not all clients knew about, and added it to both endpoints. We removed SCTs from both.October 27 16:49, we switched ca2 to chain up to the AAA Certificate Services root.October 27 18:18, we ramped up probes to be included from 1% to 10% of all challenge pages served on non-paying customer zones.With those caveats out of the way: what do we notice? Up-to-date modern browsers are mostly patched, but bots and old browsers are not. Also embedded browsers, like Android WebView, lag behind patching with 30–40% still accepting. Over the first weekend (with the monitoring gap), we see clear evidence of patching, but afterwards we see little movement.On October 29 around 18:00 UTC, we released a detection that caught a large influx of bot traffic identifying as Chrome 150-154 on macOS. This can look like patching in the top graph, but it is actually a change in traffic classification: the same user agents show a corresponding increase in acceptance among traffic with bot signals detected in the bottom graph.Chrome 150-154 on Linux is the notable exception: its acceptance continues to decline, consistent with further patching in that cohort. Given the bot-heavy and changing traffic mix, that evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive. Otherwise, we still see little movement.Breaking down by network (ASN) we see:Across the large networks, more than half of probes still accept the compromised chain, both among traffic with no bot signals detected (top graph) and traffic with bot signals detected (bottom graph). Over the weekend we saw some patching, but afterwards the trend has been flat.The big caveat still holds: traffic is skewed by (unconfirmed) bots. But bots are also just software that need security updates. And if they’re in any way representative of overall software updates, then the picture is quite dire indeed.What can you do?Patch! Dennis Jackson has a great crowdsourced website with instructions. Especially if you’re a developer on macOS, you want to follow these instructions. If you’re a Cloudflare customer, check out last week’s blog post on what needs to be done on your end when using certain products like WARP or Tunnel.Looking aheadAt Cloudflare, we have a quick-revocation mechanism in place in some products. To bring it to more systems at Cloudflare and industry, we’re excited about projects like upki that understand a trust store can’t be a static list of root certificate authorities, but needs the ability to be quickly updated with information like revocation and certificate transparency keys. As vulnerabilities are discovered at a faster pace than ever, it is vital that they can be addressed quickly and effectively.

title: [Slack Engineering] Shipyard: How We Built Slack’s Next-Generation EC2 Platform
summary: Over the past few years, we’ve been on a journey to modernise how we run Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) instances at Slack. In our first post, Advancing Our Chef Infrastructure, we shared how we moved from a single Chef stack to a resilient, multi-stack setup with versioned cookbook deployments and safer promotion workflows. This afforded us far more reliability and operational control across tens of thousands of EC2 instances. Subsequently, in Advancing Our Chef Infrastructure: Safety Without Disruption, we tackled deployment risk without the need for teams to rewrite their cookbooks. By introducing split production environments, signal-based Chef runs, and smarter rollout mechanisms, we dramatically reduced the impact radius of failures while keeping our legacy platform stable. These changes allowed us to safely operate our EC2 ecosystem at scale while we plan the future at a relaxed pace. But as we kept improving, a bigger truth became clear. Even with safer rollouts, better orchestration, and stronger guardrails, the old model—continuously updating long-lived EC2 instances—was hitting its limits. Service-level deployments were tricky, infrastructure drift was inevitable, and coordinating changes across multiple layers added complexity. Containers solved this for some classes of workloads, but not everything could migrate easily. We needed a new approach—one that brought modern deployment practices like immutability, progressive rollouts, and automated safety directly to EC2 instances. Enter Shipyard. Shipyard is Slack’s next-generation EC2 platform. It treats infrastructure as deployable artifacts rather than endlessly mutable instances. It gives teams service-level deployment primitives, tight integration with our build and orchestration systems, and the confidence to update infrastructure with the same safety and predictability we expect from modern app delivery platforms. In this post—the third chapter of our journey—we’ll explain why we built Shipyard, the principles behind its design, and how it represents a fundamental shift in how we think about running EC2 instances at Slack. What Shipyard Provides Shipyard is designed to bring modern infrastructure principles to EC2 instances while preserving the flexibility teams expect from EC2. Rather than focusing on configuration management as the center of the system, Shipyard shifts responsibility toward build pipelines, deployable artifacts, and automated safety mechanisms. Some of the key capabilities of the platform include: Multi-Architecture and Multi-OS Support The platform is designed from the start to support multiple CPU architectures, including both AMD64 and ARM-based Graviton instances, with support for multiple operating systems such as Ubuntu, RHEL, and Amazon Linux. This flexibility allows teams to optimize for cost, performance, or compatibility without needing separate platform implementations. Shipyard is particularly valuable for workloads that cannot migrate to containers, such as infrastructure components, Kubernetes worker nodes, and our egress network stacks. Metrics-Driven Deployments with Safety Controls Each service integrates with our deployment orchestration system called Gondola to enable progressive rollouts with metric based automated safety checks. Deployments can automatically halt based on service health signals, or automated rollback to previous known good versions. Fast and Predictable Provisioning Shipyard uses a layered image approach, inspired by how containers work. A shared “golden” base image provides common infrastructure components, and service-specific images are built on top of that foundation. This minimizes work at launch time, so instances can come online quickly and predictably across regions. Simplified Configuration Management One of the biggest architectural shifts is how we use configuration management. Previously, instances would run scheduled Chef jobs that periodically checked and reapplied configuration, so any manual or unexpected changes would be reverted back to the desired state. In the new model, configuration is applied during well-defined lifecycle phases like image baking and initial provisioning, rather than being continuously enforced in the background. Configuration tools are mainly used to deploy services, not to constantly modify the entire system. This reduces background load, avoids unintended overwrites, and makes system behavior much easier to reason about, since instances aren’t continuously changing over time. Real-Time Inventory and Fleet Visibility Shipyard comes with a new inventory system called Peekaboo, giving us near real-time visibility into the state of our EC2 fleet. Instead of relying on Chef Server as the source of truth, Peekaboo taps directly into cloud events and instance metadata, providing better telemetry across environments. It can even track instances from non-Shipyard deployments, giving us a complete view of the entire fleet in one place. We built Peekaboo using AWS EventBridge, OpenSearch, and Lambda. It has everything teams need: a UI to explore the fleet, an API for integrations, and a command-line interface (CLI) for quick command-line checks. By centralising this information, it removes the guesswork and gives us a single place to view and manage EC2 instances. Short-Lived, Continuously Refreshed Instances To keep our EC2 instances secure and truly immutable, each instance has a limited lifespan and is automatically rotated on a regular schedule. This means our fleets are always fresh; potential vulnerabilities have less time to cause issues, and teams focus on replacing instances rather than making in-place changes. Golden Base Images: Introducing slack-zero At the foundation of the Shipyard is a shared base image called “slack-zero.” This is the core machine image built by Slack’s Compute Platform Team and maintained collaboratively with our security and monitoring teams. The slack-zero image contains: Operating system baseline and hardening Networking and service discovery configuration Monitoring and security agents Common tooling and foundational system configuration You can think of slack-zero similarly to how teams use a base Docker image or how we start from a vendor-supplied Ubuntu image and layer additional components on top. It provides a standardised, trusted foundation that every service inherits, while still allowing teams to customize their own runtime environment on top of it. Base images are treated as immutable but ephemeral. When foundational components need to change—such as a security patch, monitoring update, or networking improvement—a new slack-zero image is produced. Downstream service images can then rebuild on top of the updated base to inherit the latest fixes and improvements. To build slack-zero, we use AWS Image Builder rather than Packer. Image Builder provides several built-in advantages over our previous approach with Packer, including: Lifecycle Management: Old AMIs are automatically cleaned up using lifecycle policies, helping reduce storage costs. AWS System Manager (SSM) Parameter Publishing: Each new slack-zero image updates an SSM parameter that indicates the latest available AMI for an account. Service pipelines read this parameter to ensure they always build on the most up-to-date base. Event-Driven Automation: When a slack-zero image finishes baking successfully, EventBridge and Lambda automatically trigger downstream pipelines in service owner accounts so dependent images can be rebuilt. Built-in Testing: Before an AMI is published, Image Builder launches temporary instances and runs validation tests. This ensures every image is verified before distribution, reducing risk and increasing confidence in production rollouts. Together, these capabilities allow us to continuously evolve the platform foundation while keeping adoption friction low for service teams. Service Images Each service team builds its own AMIs using slack-zero as the foundation. This allows teams to control their runtime environment while inheriting standardized platform components maintained by the platform organization. Service image pipelines define: What software is installed How the service is configured What happens during instance initialisation for this service Because most configuration is baked directly into the image, instances launch quickly and consistently, minimizing configuration drift and ensuring predictable behavior across the fleet. By combining the immutable slack-zero base with service-specific layers, Shipyard provides both platform stability and team-level flexibility, enabling services to innovate safely without sacrificing operational consistency. Baking and Provisioning Shipyard separates instance preparation into two distinct phases: baking and provisioning. During the bake phase, we install packages and include configuration that is consistent across environments. This ensures every instance starts from a fully prepared, known-good state with the majority of work already completed before launch. Environment-specific settings—such as secrets, regional configuration, or deployment metadata—are applied during the provisioning phase when the instance boots. This step is intentionally lightweight and typically involves only dropping configuration, retrieving secrets, and starting services. By moving heavy operations like package installation into the bake phase, instances can become operational in seconds rather than minutes. This fast startup time is critical for scaling events, rolling deployments, and automated instance replacement. This provisioning model provides a strong balance of consistency, speed, and flexibility: images deliver a stable baseline, while minimal provisioning adapts instances to their runtime environment without introducing drift. Deployments and Fleet Updates When teams need to roll out changes, they build a new Amazon Machine Instance (AMI) and then run their deployment pipeline to roll it out. Instead of patching existing instances, fleets are updated through controlled replacements, keeping everything consistent and predictable. For Auto Scaling Groups (ASGs), we use AWS Instance Refresh, and Kubernetes worker fleets use Karpenter for lifecycle-driven updates. Services with special deployment needs can use alternative rollout executors. Our global deployment orchestrator, Gondola, supports these patterns, giving teams flexibility while keeping a consistent deployment experience. Emergency Fixes and Rapid Deployment Pathways For urgent situations, the platform allows targeted configuration changes on running instances, but these are meant for emergencies only. Affected instances are expected to be replaced afterward via regular deployment pipelines. Our emergency workflows use AWS Systems Manager with a predefined document to run selected Chef recipes, letting teams quickly apply critical fixes. Once stable, instances are cycled to return to the intended immutable state. What Do Customer Pipelines Look Like? Customer pipelines in Shipyard can have multiple stages, giving teams flexibility to design them around their service and operational needs. Each stage in Gondola represents a deployable unit, such as an ASG, a Kubernetes cluster, or a group of EC2 instances. For example, the Egress Team runs separate canary and production ASGs in each availability zone, with deployment stages ordered so updates flow sequentially. Gondola updates each stage, monitors key metrics, and rolls back automatically if problems are detected, preventing issues from spreading. This staged approach, combined with Shipyard’s fast provisioning and immutable AMIs, lets teams safely deploy complex updates at scale while maintaining observability and control. What Happens in the Gondola Stage? When Gondola builds an artifact, it produces a deployable package for a service with two main parts: The AMI to roll out across the fleet The Chef artifact containing versioned recipes associated with a Git commit Gondola treats these together as a single deployable unit. Each stage uses a service-defined executor to perform the rollout: ASG-based deployments: The executor updates the launch template with the new AMI and configuration. Chef code is packaged to Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3), and new instances use a baked-in bootstrapper to fetch the correct artifact and run the relevant recipes. Configuration metadata ensures only the right configuration is applied. Kubernetes worker fleets: The executor tells Karpenter which AMI to use and provides the same configuration metadata. Nodes bootstrap in the same way, ensuring consistent provisioning. For services with special deployment needs, Gondola makes it easy to add new executors. This lets Shipyard support different deployment models while keeping artifact handling and provisioning consistent and predictable. By combining AMI updates, versioned configuration artifacts, and metadata-driven bootstrapping, Gondola ensures every instance gets the correct software and configuration for its role, no matter how it’s deployed. Simple Pipeline Shared Responsibility Shipyard’s layered image model is built on a clear shared responsibility between platform teams and service teams. The Compute, Security, and Monitoring teams manage the base layer, making sure it includes all global infrastructure components, security patches, and essential configurations. Service teams then build their own AMIs on top of this base, adding the software and settings specific to their service. Whenever the Compute team rolls out a fix or update—whether it’s a security patch, a monitoring agent update, or a networking change—service teams are responsible for incorporating the updated base into their own AMIs. This way, every service image automatically benefits from the latest improvements and security fixes from the shared base. This approach lets each team focus on what they do best while keeping the fleet consistent, secure, and reliable. The diagram below illustrates how the base and service layers work together and highlights where each team’s responsibilities lie. A Caveat on Immutability While Shipyard instances are mostly immutable, there is an important exception: secrets. Each instance runs the Consul Template service, which allows us to roll out updated secrets from Vault without cycling the fleet. This means that, although packages and configurations are fixed at bake time, sensitive data like credentials or certificates can still be updated dynamically. Our infrastructure is semi-immutable: the core system and service layers remain consistent, but critical runtime secrets can be refreshed safely as needed. This approach balances stability, predictability, and security across the fleet. The Reaper The Reaper evaluates two primary inputs. First, it consumes signals from external systems—such as security tooling or AWS EC2 events—that indicate an instance may no longer be in its desired state and should be considered “tainted.” Second, The Reaper performs periodic checks to identify instances that have been running for longer than their allowed lifespan. When either condition is met, the instance is scheduled for replacement according to its service policies. This approach helps reduce configuration drift, limit exposure to vulnerabilities, and reinforce the principle that infrastructure should be updated by redeploying rather than modifying systems in place. The result is a platform that is more reliable, auditable, and predictable. For example, while manual remote access remains available for emergency scenarios, manually accessing a production-class node will generate a signal that marks the instance for eventual replacement, supporting our immutable infrastructure goals. The Reaper also integrates with Peekaboo to track instance age across the fleet. Once a node reaches its maximum lifespan, it follows the same graceful replacement workflow. Looking ahead, we plan to make the system more context-aware so that only meaningful changes—such as software updates or configuration drift—trigger replacement, while read-only or low-risk actions do not create unnecessary churn. Taming the Reaper The Reaper is designed not only to enforce lifecycle policies, but also to give teams control over how replacements occur. Built-in rate limiting allows service owners to define how many instances can be replaced at a time, scoped by service, region, or availability zone, preventing sudden capacity impacts. For emergency situations, we provide a global pause mechanism—the “big red button.” By placing a control object in S3, teams can temporarily halt all Reaper activity across the fleet. This provides a safe and immediate way to stop instance cycling during incidents or periods of elevated risk. We also provide a CLI that allows service owners to manage rate limits, inspect configuration, and activate or release the global pause when needed. In addition, controlled access mechanisms such as short-lived SSH certificate workflows can be used for break-glass scenarios where deeper investigation is required, while still maintaining overall lifecycle safety commitments. Together, these capabilities make the Reaper both predictable and controllable—enforcing instance immutability by default while giving teams the visibility and safeguards they need to operate confidently. How Do We Test Changes? Both platform teams and service owners need a safe way to test cookbook changes before merging a pull request, so we built a system called Ship Quick—a developer workflow that runs a realistic bake-and-provision test on real infrastructure. Developers run a CLI command from their cookbook repo, where a YAML file defines the test cases. Ship Quick packages the cookbook, uploads it to S3, and sends a workflow message to a queue. A fleet of worker instances—managed by a lightweight process called Longshoremen—picks up the job, detaches from its Auto Scaling Group, runs the Chef workflow, streams logs back to the CLI, and then terminates (unless the developer chooses to keep it for debugging). We run Longshorem in two separate worker fleets because of how our bootstrapping works. The vanilla Ubuntu fleet is used to bake and test the base slack-zero image—it can’t build on top of itself, so starting from a clean Ubuntu AMI is required. The slack-zero fleet is for service team cookbooks, which depend on the pre-baked slack-zero AMI. Running tests from this fleet ensures provisioning is validated against the same foundation used in production. Splitting the fleets this way helps ensure each layer is tested against the correct base. Both fleets scale automatically with demand, and slack-zero workers are continuously updated to the latest images so tests always reflect the current production environment. Teams that build images in their own AWS accounts can also provision dedicated worker fleets and route Ship Quick jobs to them, ensuring isolation while keeping the same workflow. What’s Next? So far, Shipyard has been working really well for short-lived services, and we’re actively onboarding teams from the legacy EC2 platform. Our next challenge is long-lived instances—things like Slack’s data nodes, singleton services like GitHub Enterprise, or third-party business technology instances such as Atlassian JIRA. These can’t be cycled quickly, so we need ways to patch and update them safely while ensuring the Reaper handles them correctly. We’re collaborating closely with service teams to develop new deploy executors in Gondola for these longer-lived workloads. As more teams adopt Shipyard, we’ll keep iterating on tooling, developer workflows, and the overall deployment experience to meet the platform’s diverse needs. Future posts in this series will cover the challenges we encounter as Shipyard evolves and take a closer look at its components—including the Shipyard API, image pipelines, developer workflows, and our inventory system. Stay tuned!

title: [Pulumi] Running Pulumi Neo in a Docker Sandbox: workshop recap
summary: The more an agent can do on its own, the more infrastructure work you can hand it, as long as its limits hold when it gets something wrong. In April, they didn’t hold for PocketOS. A coding agent on a routine staging task deleted the company’s production volume in 9 seconds. According to founder Jer Crane’s account, it used an API token it found in an unrelated file. Its explanation afterward: “I guessed that deleting a staging volume via the API would be scoped to staging only. I didn’t verify.” Railway recovered the data two days later. The agent had been told not to. “System prompts are advisory, not enforcing,” Crane wrote afterward. If the prompt can’t stop an agent, the limits have to sit where the agent can’t negotiate with them. That was the premise of Neo in a Docker Sandbox, the workshop Adam Gordon Bell and I ran with Mike Coleman from Docker. So we gave Pulumi Neo two layers. The first is a Docker Sandbox. Neo runs in its own microVM and reaches only the files and hosts we allow. The Pulumi token gets injected by a proxy on the way out, so Neo never holds the real credential. The second is Pulumi itself, which decides what Neo may change and when it has to ask. With both in place, you can let Neo work without approving every step. For why YOLO mode belongs in a sandbox at all, see my August post. Mike Coleman is a Principal Solutions Architect at Docker. His running joke is that agents “want to be helpful”. It happens in his own demos: Mike Coleman I talk to people about agents a lot. They just really want to please you. I don’t know how many times I’ve done a demo  governance for MCP servers, and I’ll be like, “Can you write to my Notion page?” And there will be a policy applied to the sandbox that says it can’t. But I have a connector enabled in Claude somewhere. And it’s like, “Well, not with that MCP server, but I can use this thing over here to do it.” Mike’s answer is to close those doors before the agent finds them: Mike Coleman The more you can create an environment where these alternate avenues are roadblocked, the safer you’re gonna be with agentic workflows. That’s where we’re coming at with the sandboxes: how do we take something that is as powerful as an agent, allow it to run as close to its full potential as possible, but avoid a bunch of catastrophic things. A deleted database scores the same as a failed task Adam’s explanation of why a capable agent does this starts with how it’s trained. Agents got good at code fast. METR measures the length of software task, in human hours, that a model can finish on its own half the time, and it has doubled every few months. Source: METR, Time Horizon 1.1. Behind that improvement is reinforcement learning on coding tasks. The model gets a task, tries it many times in a throwaway sandbox, and each attempt is scored pass or fail. Every attempt runs in a sandbox that resets afterward. In that sandbox, nothing it does can go worse than failing the task. There is no downside bigger than a zero, so the model never learns that some actions are worse than others. Adam Gordon Bell In the training environment, if you solve a task, you get one point. If you don’t solve the task, you get zero. But there’s no in-between. If you destroy the entire repo, if you delete prod, that’s the same thing. You got the task or you failed the task. There’s no asymmetric downside. Production is different. Adam Gordon Bell  existing benchmarks, no matter what you do, the worst you can get on any task is: you didn’t complete it. But in the real world, some tasks have a catastrophic downside. Published coding-agent training runs such as DeepSWE and SWE-Universe use that 1-or-0 reward. Adam’s answer is a matrix with reversibility on one axis and blast radius on the other. Training happens in the top row. Production work lives in the bottom right. Adam’s rule is that agents can act on their own when there are no side effects, when someone reviews the change, or when there’s an easy way to recover. The PocketOS agent was working in staging, which felt safe. The token it found let it leave staging without anyone noticing. Infrastructure as code moves production work toward those conditions. An agent’s change becomes a diff you can preview, check against policy, and review before it reaches the cloud. Six questions before an agent gets your cloud account Before an agent gets a cloud account, six questions: Engin Diri Who is this agent acting as? What is it allowed to change? And when does it stop and ask? That last one has a history. The human-in-the-loop pattern was very, very big at the start, and everybody was like, “Hey, there should always be a human approving stuff.” Then it shifted when everything came around to the Ralph loop, loop engineering and so on. Asking was considered something which slows you down. Still, maybe very important. Where does the agent actually run? Which credentials does it hold? And what stops it when it goes wrong? Keep these questions as a loose guardrail. Six questions before an agent gets a cloud account. Pulumi answers who, what, when, and what stops it. The sandbox answers where, and it splits the credentials question with Pulumi ESC (Environments, Secrets, and Configuration). Pulumi controls that live outside the prompt pulumi neo runs Neo in your terminal (Essentials, Pro, and Enterprise editions). Its controls live in Pulumi: Neo runs as you. It uses your pulumi login and role-based access control (RBAC) permissions, and its file and shell tool calls run locally, inside the sandbox. Approval mode sets when it asks. --approval-mode manual, the default, asks before every tool call, balanced only before pulumi up, and auto never. Read-only blocks Pulumi Cloud writes only. With --permission-mode read-only, Neo can’t trigger writes such as pulumi up, but it can still open ESC environments and reach the cloud accounts behind them. To keep it out of an environment, don’t grant your user or role environment:open on it. protect: true guards against accidental deletes. A deployment that would delete a protected resource fails. protect: false, pulumi state unprotect, or --ignore-protect still gets past it. Pulumi Policies blocks unsafe changes. Mandatory policies in a preventative policy group (Pro and Enterprise editions) run on every pulumi preview and pulumi up, Neo’s included, and stop a violating change before anything reaches the cloud. The workshop’s pack included s3-no-public-acl. Pulumi ESC replaces stored cloud keys. It mints short-lived AWS credentials through OpenID Connect (OIDC) for each run. They still reach the CLI, so they limit a leak’s damage rather than prevent it. What a Docker Sandbox isolates Each agent gets its own microVM, kernel, and Docker Engine. Only the workspace is mounted (plus a read-only skills store for supported agents), but SSH agent forwarding is on by default. All outbound TCP goes through a host proxy that injects proxy-managed credentials such as the Pulumi token. The sbx CLI and local sandboxes are free; centralized sandbox, network, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) controls are part of Docker’s paid AI Governance. What changed in Docker Sandboxes since August Secrets are global and reach running sandboxes. Since v0.38.0 (August 6), sbx secret set pulumi covers every sandbox whose kit asks for it. Since v0.45.0 (September 21), changing a global secret updates running sandboxes without a restart. Sandbox environment files (experimental). An sbxenv.yaml captures a sandbox’s agent, kits, workspace, ports, and credentials for sbx env run. Mike compared it to a dev container definition. Docker now says to keep the file under version control but outside the mounted workspace, because it can run host commands. Cloud sandboxes (experimental). sbx --cloud run claude runs the sandbox in Docker’s cloud, so it keeps going after you close the laptop. It needs sbx 0.45.0 or later and a pay-as-you-go Docker Agentic Platform subscription. New signups get a one-time $250 compute credit, instead of $25, through October 31, 2026. Running Neo inside a Docker Sandbox Every script is in the workshop repo. Store the token on the host, allow ghcr.io/dirien/ in kit.allowedSources, then start the sandbox from my kit plus a mixin for the demo’s AWS region: sbx secret set pulumi sbx run --name neo-demo --kit ./01-sandbox/region-kit \ ghcr.io/dirien/infrastructure-sandbox-kit:v0.10.0 ./02-app Neo isn’t a built-in sbx agent, so the sandbox opens a shell, where pulumi whoami -v works through the injected token while the variable holds a placeholder: echo "$PULUMI_ACCESS_TOKEN" proxy-managed From the host, the workshop’s boundaries.sh checks a host the kit doesn’t allow and one it does: sbx policy check network --sandbox neo-demo ifconfig.me sbx policy check network --sandbox neo-demo api.pulumi.com Under Balanced or Locked Down the first is denied, and sbx policy log neo-demo shows what the proxy refused. The Open preset allows all traffic. Without organization governance, a request that matches no rule is blocked and queued for your approval (sbx policy approval ls). The allow-list is an excerpt. Then start Neo: pulumi neo Inside the sandbox, I think auto approval mode is defensible for throwaway work. But allowed hosts, AWS included, still receive whatever Neo sends, and ESC’s short-lived credentials reach the CLI, so keep the Pulumi controls on. The last step, Neo trying to tear the stack down and protect: true refusing, didn’t make it into the live session. Where to start In an informal poll at the end of the workshop, 8 of the 11 people who voted said they don’t use a sandbox for their agents. If that’s you, start closed: pick Locked Down when the first start asks for a network preset. Read the denials in the terminal dashboard (sbx with no subcommand) or with sbx policy log, then approve them or add rules with sbx policy allow network <host>. On the Pulumi side, start Neo with balanced approval near production, so it works freely but asks before pulumi up, and back the stack with an ESC environment that uses OIDC. workshop virtual Neo in a Docker Sandbox: Using Pulumi’s Coding Agent for All Things Infra Safely and Securely 16 Sep Join Docker and Pulumi to run Neo, Pulumi’s infrastructure coding agent, inside a Docker Sandbox and turn plain-English requests into real cloud infrastructure. with Adam Gordon Bell, Engin Diri, Mike Coleman Beginner Register If you sandbox your agents differently, tell me how in the Pulumi Community Slack.

title: [Docker] Win the Agentic Era, Together: Introducing the Docker Navigator Partner Program
summary: Over the past year, almost every conversation I’ve had with a partner has ended in the same place. Their customers are moving AI agents out of the lab and into production, and the moment they do, the question changes. It stops being “Can we build this?” and becomes “Can we trust it, secure it, and govern it?” The partners who can answer that second set of questions are the partners customers keep. Today, we are launching the Docker Navigator Partner Program to help you become that partner. This post explains what we’ve built, why we built it around AI governance, and how you can get the most from it. Why “Navigator” AI adoption is not following a normal technology curve. Every team, every vendor, every model provider, and every hyperscaler is racing to ship agentic capability, and no single company sees the whole stack. Identity, observability, supply chain security, MCP gateways, models, and clouds are each building their piece. What enterprises are missing is a trusted, common layer that lets those pieces work together safely. That’s Docker’s role. Docker is where agents, models, and tools actually run: vertically integrated where it matters, and horizontally open to everything our customers already use. We describe it as being the Trusted Navigator for the agentic era; the constant that helps customers make sense of a landscape moving faster than any one team can track. Partners are how that promise reaches customers. Whether you build technology, run a cloud, deliver services, or sell through the channel, you extend our reach and turn the Docker platform into a complete, governable stack. So the program carries the same name, and its tiers describe the journey a partner takes with us. Three tiers, one partner journey Every partner in the Docker Navigator Partner Program is navigating the agentic era with Docker. The tiers mark how far along that journey you are, and the top tier carries the program’s name on purpose: it’s the title you earn when you have shown you can navigate it for customers. Crew is where every partnership starts: signed, onboarded, portal profile complete, first opportunities registered. Explorer partners are enabled and certified, actively selling and co-marketing AI governance solutions with us. Navigator partners are our most strategic: co-selling with Docker, embedded in joint account plans, co-authoring reference architectures, and leading customers through the agentic era alongside us. A Navigator is a partner Docker would put in front of its own customers. If you’re already a Docker partner, you enter the new program at the tier that matches your status today. Nothing is taken away, and your tier is protected until 30 April 2027 while we work with you on the requirements. What you get for navigating with us We designed the benefits around one principle: the more you invest in building a governed AI practice on Docker, the more Docker invests in you. At the top tier, that means: a dedicated partner success manager and joint account planning with quarterly business reviews; deal registrations protection; priority access to betas and a dedicated product roadmap briefing each quarter; co-funded marketing (MDF), joint campaigns, and co-published customer stories; speaking slots at Docker events and a seat on our Partner Advisory Board. The commercial model rewards what you bring: Partner-sourced, registered deals earn the highest discount at every tier. From launch until 31 January 2027, every approved AI Governance deal registration earns an additional 10 points on top of your tier discount through the AI Governance Growth Incentive, on deals that close by 30 April 2027. If you’re working on an AI governance opportunity today, register it. Everything lives in one place: the new Docker Navigator Partner Portal, where you register deals, take the free Docker Partner Sales Certification, request MDF, download assets, and track your progress against your tier in real time. The ecosystem is the product No one wins the agentic era alone, and Docker has spent much of 2026 demonstrating our belief in a collaborative ecosystem and approach. For example, in September, Docker became a founding member of the Blueprint Alliance alongside Okta, AWS, CrowdStrike, Databricks, Google Cloud, Lovable, Proofpoint, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Wiz and Zscaler, with GE Appliances and World Central Kitchen serving as strategic advisors. Announced at Oktane in Las Vegas, the Alliance has agreed on a shared architecture for securing AI agents, built around four questions every enterprise is asking: Where are my agents? What can they do? What are they doing? How do I respond? Our part is the environment where agents execute: isolation, runtime governance, and a secure supply chain that extends trust beyond the model to the place the agent runs. What our partners say “In the agentic era, you can’t govern what you can’t see. Docker gives teams a secure, consistent runtime for AI agents, and Datadog gives them visibility into how those agents actually behave in production including the tool calls, the costs, the failure modes. Together, that’s a complete picture. The Docker Navigator Partner Program gives our joint partners a clear path to deliver it.“ Uday Tennety Head of Technology Partnerships, Datadog “AI agents are writing, containerizing, and shipping code faster than security teams can manually review. Snyk and Docker have spent years helping developers ship securely — and now we’re taking that further. Together, we’re giving teams the ability to run agents in isolated environments with security testing built in from the start, so every dependency, every generated artifact, and every tool an agent can reach is assessed before it ever touches production. The Docker Navigator Partner Program is how that gets to the broader ecosystem.“ Carey Stanton SVP Business Development, Snyk Watch: why Docker, and the market opportunity for partners (20 minutes) Mat Velloso, our Chief Product Officer, and I recorded a 20-minute conversation for partners on why Docker sits where the agentic era is being decided, where the AI governance opportunity is opening up, and what it means for your business. It’s the fastest way to get your sales and technical teams on the same page. After you log in to the Docker Navigator Partner Portal, you can watch the recording here. Three things to do this week Log in to the Docker Navigator Partner Portal (https://partner.docker.com/) and complete your company profile. Register the AI governance opportunities you’re already working on so they qualify for the incentive. Book a session with your Docker partner manager to agree to your account plan for the first half of 2027. Not yet a partner? Start at https://www.docker.com/partners/register/. This is a new program for Docker, and we’re humble enough to know we won’t have everything perfect on day one. We want your feedback and input. Tell us what’s missing. We’ll listen, we’ll be open with you, and we’ll invest in your success. Let’s win the agentic era, together.
